newsitem.title: INDIA: Young leader challenges India Congress chief.
newsitem.headline: Young leader challenges India Congress chief.

text.p: Youthful upstart Rajesh Pilot on Tuesday entered the race for the Congress party presidency, setting up an uncommon battle for control of India's oldest political machine.

Joined by vocal supporters, Pilot launched a campaign targeted at the current party president, veteran Sitaram Kesri, and called for young blood and a drive to clean up a party tainted by corruption scandals.

By throwing down the gauntlet for the June 9 election of party president, Pilot virtually assured the first public leadership contest in 20 years in a party accustomed to selecting leaders in backroom deals.
"Inner-party democracy is often shied away from in the name of breeding factionalism," Pilot said in a statement.
Pilot, 50, a former air force officer and junior minister, is considered an outspoken, ambitious leader who has modern ideas and strong roots in village politics.
Wearing a tomato-red farmer's turban, Pilot marched to the Congress office as hundreds of supporters from his rural constituency beat drums and sang folk songs.
Kesri took charge in September last year, four months after Congress suffered its worst electoral defeat.

Congress, which had ruled India for all but five years since independence in 1947, still wields considerable influence as it lends crucial support to Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's centre-left United Front coalition.
But Kesri, 77, stirred criticism in his party in March when he suddenly forced the United Front to abandon then prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, triggering a three-week national political crisis.

On Monday, Abdul Rahman Antulay, a leader from the western state of Maharashtra, entered the party leadership race but said he was willing to stand down in favour of anyone else so long as Kesri faced a contest.
Kesri was expected to announce his candidacy on Wednesday, the deadline for filing nomination papers. Other contenders were expected to emerge to challenge Congress's history of closed-door politics.

"All functionaries and leaders, including the president, should be directly elected, and no attempt should be made to follow any other procedure such as elections by consensus or appointments by nominations at level of the party," Pilot said.
Kesri was named party president in September when former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao stepped down after being accused in three corruption cases. He says he is innocent.
Kesri's appointment has yet to be ratified by the party's plenary, the All India Congress Committee.
